records.toxicity_detail: NC State's page for Gerbera jamesonii carries the tags "#non-toxic for cats", "#non-toxic for horses" and "#non-toxic for dogs" (horse tag kept separate from the cat and dog tags). The full tag list on the page is: #showy flowers #fall interest #fantz #summer flowers #pink flowers #non-toxic for cats #non-toxic for horses #non-toxic for dogs #mass planting #perennial #spring flowers #container plant #border planting #HS304 #herbaceous perennial #fall color #partial shade tolerant #long bloom season #fpp. Plant Type on the page is Annual, Herbaceous Perennial. The page has no Poison block, no symptom list, no poison-part list and no handling warning. It says nothing about eating the plant.
unknowns: NC State (plants.ces.ncsu.edu) is the anchor source. RHS's dedicated page (https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/70682/gerbera-jamesonii/details) agrees on the name (subtitle Barberton daisy, Name Status Correct) and on full sun, and diverges as follows: its Position lists Full sun only, while NC State's structured Light field also lists Partial Shade, kept here because the only source leaving it out is RHS, a UK source, not a second North American structured field; its Moisture field reads Well–drained alone, a bare well-drained that sets no drainage token and gives no watering instruction; its Max Height is 0.5-1 metres (19.7-39.4 in) and its Max Spread 0.1-0.5 metres (3.9-19.7 in), against NC State's 12-18 in and 12-15 in, and NC State's species Dimensions block is used; its pH reads Acid or Alkaline or Neutral, which gives no numeric bound; its hardiness rating H1C is not a damage-onset temperature; it carries no toxicity, pollinator or edibility statement. MoBot's Plant Finder could not be loaded from this machine (SSL certificate error), and no UF/IFAS EDIS sheet for this species was found (FP228-FP231, after the Gazania sheets, return 404).
Toxicity: NC State's non-toxic tags are for cats, dogs and horses. The page has no Poison block and no statement on edibility, so is_edible is null.

Soil drainage: NC State's structured Soil Drainage is Good Drainage alone; the prose says moist, well-drained soil and warns that soggy soils can cause root rot, so soil_drainage is moderate. 'It should be kept moist' is a watering statement, used only for water_regime.

water_regime keep_moist rests on one NC State watering sentence; NC State has no structured Water field. RHS's dedicated page gives no watering statement; its Moisture field reads Well–drained alone, a soil descriptor disclosed here as a counterpoint, not a watering cadence. MoBot could not be loaded.

Sun: NC State's Light field lists Full sun (6 or more hours) and Partial Shade (2-6 hours); direct_sun_hours_max is null because no species-specific prose gives an hour figure. The prose also advises protection from hot afternoon sun in hot climates.

soil_base garden_bed rests on NC State's garden-soil preference ('This plant prefers moist, well-drained soil rich in organic matter in full sun.'), its Soil Texture field (Clay, High Organic Matter, Loam (Silt)) and its 'Use this plant in borders, containers or in groups' sentence. NC State also lists Container and Houseplants as Landscape Locations, and RHS's Cultivation text calls it 'ideal for patio containers grown in a peat-free, loam-based potting compost (JI No.2)'.

Left null for lack of admissible evidence: temperatures, chill damage, humidity, indoor light, soil pH, dry-down target, check depth, watering day estimates, fertilizer interval, months and strength (the page says only 'fertilized lightly', not a dilution fraction), and pollinator attraction (no Attracts field on the page).
Houseplants appears as a Landscape Location value on NC State, but the page gives no indoor culture guidance beyond overwintering a potted plant in a cool frost-free location with bright light.

Size comes from NC State's Dimensions block: Height 1 ft 0 in to 1 ft 6 in (12-18 in) and Width 1 ft 0 in to 1 ft 3 in (12-15 in). The page's cultivar notes (for example 'Pink and White Linosa' at 12 to 18 inches) were not used.

records.name_note: Admissible dedicated pages split on the lead common name. NC State's page is headed by the scientific name, and its Common Name(s) list, in the same order as its page-title parenthetical, reads Egyptian Starcluster, Egyptian Star Cluster, Egyptian Star flower, Pentas and Star Cluster; its description calls the plant Egyptian Star Flower. UF/IFAS's fact sheet gives its common names as 'pentas, Egyptian starcluster'. Pentas is the bare genus name, so the catalog lands Egyptian Starcluster. RHS's page title is 'Pentas lanceolata | Egyptian star', with 'Egyptian star, Egyptian star cluster, star cluster' under Other common names.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail left null: the NC State page carries no Poison block and no Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tag, and no other admissible page naming cats or dogs was read; RHS's and UF/IFAS's pages, read at audit and landing, carry no toxicity statement either.

soil_drainage left null: NC State's Soil Drainage field lists Good Drainage and Occasionally Dry, and its prose has only a bare 'well-drained' with no moist-but-well-drained statement, so it is not fast and not clearly moderate. Read after research: RHS's Moisture field reads 'Moist but well–drained or Well–drained' and UF/IFAS says pentas 'prefers fertile, well-drained soils, regular moisture'; the audit did not propose a token from them and none was set at landing.
soil_base left null: NC State lists Soil Texture High Organic Matter and Loam (Silt) but gives no potting-mix or bed recommendation that maps to an enum token.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max left null: NC State's Soil pH field lists only 'Acid (<6.0)', an open-ended band this catalog does not read a floor or ceiling from, and RHS's pH field reads 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral', so no page read gives a numeric pH range.

water_regime is dry_surface_between from 'water consistently and allow soils to dry between watering'; the statement names no depth, so it does not support dry_thoroughly_between. water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm and the day-interval fields are null because NC State does not frame watering that way for this in-ground shrub.

outdoor_sun_exposure: NC State's Light field lists Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day) and Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours), and UF/IFAS's Light requirement reads 'plant grows in part shade/part sun', so part_shade is kept. RHS's Position reads 'Full sun', and Missouri Botanical Garden's structured field reads 'Sun: Full sun' (the auditor's browser reading, not machine-checkable here). NC State says full sun 'encourages blossoms' and that the plant 'will tolerate some shade', and Missouri Botanical Garden says 'Tolerates part shade, but best flowering in full sun.' (also the auditor's reading). direct_sun_hours_max is null: no source gives a maximum (UF/IFAS gives only a minimum, 'Plants will flower fairly well with as little as 2 to 3 hours of sun each day.'), and NC State's hour ranges are its standard light-category wording.

humidity_need high rests on the NC State sentence about indoor culture north of zone 10 ('a sunny room with high humidity'); no percentage is stated, so humidity_pct_min and humidity_pct_max are null.

Temperature, chill damage, cool rest, light foot-candles, fertilizer and is_edible fields are null: NC State gives no figures or statements for them (the 10a-11b hardiness zones are a survival rating, not a damage-onset temperature). No source addresses eating, so is_edible is null rather than false. RHS's Cultivation text gives 'Minimum temperature 7°C' for plants grown in a temperate greenhouse or in containers moved indoors over winter, a growing minimum rather than a damage-onset temperature, and UF/IFAS says only that 'Plants fertilized regularly during the growing season will continue to grow and bloom all during the warm months.', with no interval or strength; neither sets a field.

Mature size comes from NC State's Dimensions block (Height 1 ft. 0 in. - 2 ft. 0 in. = 12-24 in; Width 0 ft. 9 in. - 2 ft. 0 in. = 9-24 in). The body prose says it can reach 6 feet in its native east African environment, 'but 2 feet high with an equal spread is more likely in other environments'; the 6-foot figure is not used. The other admissible pages run larger: UF/IFAS FP465 gives 'Height: 2 to 3 feet' and 'Spread: 2 to 3 feet' and its introduction says the plant 'becomes 3 to 4 feet tall' in Florida's hardiness zones 9 through 11, and RHS gives Max Height 1.5-2.5 metres and Max Spread 0.5-1 metres. NC State's species Dimensions block is the anchor.

RHS's profile for this species is https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/80589/pentas-lanceolata/details (the ID-less URL rhs.org.uk/plants/pentas-lanceolata returns 404); its Name Status field reads 'Correct', agreeing with NC State's binomial. UF/IFAS's fact sheet FPS465/FP465 (https://edis.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/FP465) was read at landing. Missouri Botanical Garden's Plant Finder page (taxonid=286726) refuses scripted clients from this machine; the auditor read it in a browser (Common Name field 'Egyptian star flower'), and since none of its quotes can be machine-checked here it is not cited and no value or name_note sentence rests on it.
NC State page type tags include both Annual and Herbaceous Perennial/Perennial/Shrub; the species is a tropical plant treated as an annual or houseplant north of zones 10 and 11.

common_name researched as 'Egyptian Star Cluster' (the batch's spelling); landed as 'Egyptian Starcluster', the first entry of NC State's Common Name(s) list and UF/IFAS's species name, after the audit flagged that no dedicated page leads with the researched form. 'Egyptian Star Cluster' is NC State's second entry and RHS's second Other common name. No landed common_name collides with either spelling.

records.toxicity_detail: Source: NC State Plant Toolbox page for Dianthus chinensis, plus RHS's dedicated page for the handling warning. NC State summary line: "This plant has low severity poison characteristics." NC State's Problems field lists four tags: Poisonous to Humans, Problem for Cats, Problem for Dogs, Problem for Horses. toxic_to_pets rests only on the separate Problem for Cats and Problem for Dogs tags; Problem for Horses is a separate animal and does not count toward it. NC State gives no cat- or dog-specific symptoms, severity or poison part. Its detailed "Poisonous to Humans" block is human-scoped and reads: Poison Severity: Low. Poison Symptoms: "No reports of ingestion. Skin irritation reported from contact with clove pinks; minor and lasts only a few minutes, and vomiting." Poison Toxic Principle: Triterpenoid saponins. Causes Contact Dermatitis: Yes. Poison Part: Leaves. Disclosure: that symptom sentence names clove pinks rather than Dianthus chinensis; the same block on this species' page states Causes Contact Dermatitis: Yes. NC State's Plant Type field lists Annual, Herbaceous Perennial, Poisonous. Handling warning, RHS Potentially harmful field: "Humans/Pets: Skin allergen; wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling.  For further information and contact numbers regarding pets, see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants"; its Pets scope names no animal, so it does not bear on toxic_to_pets. NC State's Uses (Ethnobotany) text describes Chinese herbal medicine use and says "The plants are harvested before the flowers bloom and then dried."; no admissible source says the plant is eaten as food.
unknowns: NC State Plant Toolbox, RHS (https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/74267/dianthus-chinensis-p-a/details, titled Dianthus chinensis (p,a)) and MoBot (https://plantfinder.mobot.org/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?kempercode=a574) each have a dedicated page for this species. MoBot's server fails certificate verification for non-browser clients, so MoBot quotes cannot be machine-checked, though the page renders in a browser; the auditor read there 'Common Name: pink' and 'Dianthus chinensis, commonly called China pinks, grows to as much as 30" tall and features pink to lilac flowers with fringed petals and a purple eye.', and no value rests on that reading. Clemson HGIC returned 403. RHS corroborates Position 'Full sun', Moisture 'Well–drained', pH 'Neutral or Alkaline' and the name 'Chinese pink'; its Name Status reads Unresolved.

is_houseplant false: NC State says only that "It is sometimes offered as a potted florist plant." and describes China pinks as biennials or short-lived perennials primarily grown as annuals; its Plant Type field lists Annual, Herbaceous Perennial and Poisonous. RHS's suggested planting locations include Patio and container plants, Bedding, and Flower borders and beds, MoBot's Uses read "Beds and borders. Edgings. Group or mass near doors or walkways. Containers." (the auditor's browser reading), and no admissible source calls it a houseplant.

toxic_to_pets is true on the strength of NC State's separate Problem for Cats and Problem for Dogs tags only; no source text gives pet-specific symptoms, severity or poison part. The human-scoped block says severity Low, poison part Leaves, and its symptom sentence is about clove pinks. Problem for Horses is listed separately.

soil_drainage moderate is a judgement call: NC State gives Good Drainage and Occasionally Dry, prose says average well-drained soils with dry to medium moisture, and warns of crown rot and rust if the soil is poorly drained. There is no sharp or sandy requirement (Soil Texture lists Clay, Loam, Sand), so not fast; no source asks for consistently wet soil, so not moisture_retentive.
soil_base garden_bed is inferred from NC State's in-ground cultural prose; the page also tags it as a container plant.

soil_ph_max left null because NC State's Soil pH field lists both Alkaline (>8.0), which is open-ended, and Neutral (6.0-8.0). soil_ph_min 6.0 is the floor of the lowest band listed; acid soils are not listed, and RHS's pH field reads 'Neutral or Alkaline'.

water_regime and the day-interval and dry-down fields left null: NC State has no watering statement or structured water field, only soil-drainage tags and the soil description, which are not a watering instruction.

outdoor_sun_exposure: NC State lists Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day) and Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours), mapped to full_sun and part_shade. Prose adds afternoon shade in warmer climates. direct_sun_hours_max left null because the hour figures are the site-wide light-category legend, not species prose.
Temperature, chill damage, humidity, light foot-candles, and fertilizing have no admissible support and are null. NC State's hardiness zones 6a-9b are not a damage-onset temperature.
is_edible null: no admissible source addresses eating this plant. The ethnobotany note describes Chinese herbal medicine use and the human poison block says no reports of ingestion.

Mature size is NC State's Dimensions block, Height 0 ft. 6 in. - 2 ft. 6 in. (6-30 in) and Width 0 ft. 6 in. - 1 ft. 0 in. (6-12 in). NC State also lists Available Space To Plant: Less than 12 inches. RHS gives Max Height and Max Spread of 0.1-0.5 metres (3.9-19.7 in); NC State's species Dimensions block is the anchor.

records.name_note: NC State's dedicated page is headed Cleome houtteana, and its Previously known as list gives Cleome hassleriana, Cleome spinosa and Tarenaya houtteana. RHS's dedicated Cleome houtteana page gives Name Status Correct, and its Synonyms field lists Cleome hassleriana and Cleome spinosa misapplied. The accepted name is Cleome houtteana. Sources split on the lead common name. RHS's browser page title reads Cleome houtteana | spider flower, and RHS lists spider plant among its other common names. NC State has no single Common Name line, only the alphabetized Common Name(s) list, which matches the title parenthetical (Cleome, Grandfather's Whiskers, Pink Queen, Spider Flower, Spider Plant, Spider's Legs). That list opens with Cleome, the bare genus name, which is not used as the common name here, and NC State's description prose opens with 'The spider plant'. Spider Plant is the landed common name of Chlorophytum comosum in this catalog, so this record lands under RHS's lead, Spider Flower, which NC State's list also carries. No Chlorophytum text was used.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's tag list for this page carries both '#non-toxic for cats' and '#non-toxic for dogs'. The full tag line reads: #drought tolerant #purple #fantz #deer resistant #leggy #rabbit resistant #well-drained soil #sticky #heat tolerant #moist soil #showy flowers #low maintenance #fall interest #humidity tolerant #fast growing #summer flowers #pink flowers #tropical feel #non-toxic for cats #non-toxic for horses #non-toxic for dogs #stormwater demo garden orange co #full sun tolerant #white flowers #annual #self-seeding #HS303. The '#non-toxic for horses' tag is separate and says nothing about cats or dogs. Plant Type is Annual. The page has no Poison block, no severity rating, no poison-part list, no symptom list and no handling warning. The tag line carries '#sticky', and the description says 'The musky odor, especially if planted in groups, is offensive to some.' Those are texture and odor notes, not toxicity findings. RHS says nothing about toxicity, so the cat and dog non-toxic scope rests on NC State's tags alone. No admissible source states anything about eating the plant.
unknowns: chill_damage_f is null: RHS's bare hardiness rating is H2 and NC State gives USDA zones 10a-11b, which are hardiness ratings and not a damage-onset temperature.

Temperature ranges (day and night), humidity, light in foot-candles and direct_sun_hours_max are null: no admissible source states them for this species. NC State's 'heat, humidity, drought and deer tolerant' and its Resistance To Challenges list are tolerance traits, not a humidity need. The 6-or-more-hours figure is only NC State's site-wide light legend.

water_regime and all watering and fertilizer fields are null: NC State uses 'moist' only to describe soil (the Soil Drainage value Moist, the #moist soil tag and 'moist well-drained soils' in the description) and gives drought and dry soil only as tolerance traits (the #drought tolerant tag and the Resistance To Challenges values Drought and Dry Soil), with no watering statement. records.name_note: Sources split on the lead common name. NC State's Common Name(s) list reads Four-o'clock then Marvel-of-Peru, in the same order as its page-title parenthetical, and its description opens 'Four-o’clock is a deciduous, semi-woody perennial in the four-o’clock family (Nyctaginaceae).' RHS's page title is 'Mirabilis jalapa | marvel of Peru' (its plant-profile subtitle renders the same name), and its Other common names field lists 'four o'clock flower' and 'four o'clock plant' among nine names. This record lands NC State's lead, Four-o'clock.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's Poison block is human-scoped (Problems: Poisonous to Humans). Page summary: "This plant has low severity poison characteristics." Poison Severity: Low. Poison Symptoms: Stomach pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea; handling of the roots may cause dermatitis. Poison Toxic Principle: Unknown. Causes Contact Dermatitis: Yes. Poison Part: Roots, Seeds. Plant Type field: Annual, Herbaceous Perennial, Poisonous. Tag line carries #poisonous alongside #weedy, #tuberous, #annual, #drought tolerant and others. Admissible sources differ on scope: NC State's Poison Part list names only Roots and Seeds, while RHS's Potentially harmful field reads "Harmful if eaten.  Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling" without naming a part. No admissible source names cats or dogs, so risk to pets is not stated.
unknowns: Keep NC State's dig-and-store advice: old plants produce large, potato-like tuberous roots that can be dug before the first freeze in the fall to store indoors and replanted in spring after the last frost; in Zone 8 or 9 the roots can stay in the ground and regrow.
Keep NC State's weedy warning: the plants can self-seed vigorously and become weedy.

toxic_to_pets left null: no admissible source names cats or dogs. NC State's Poison block is human-scoped (Poisonous to Humans) and the page carries no cat or dog tag; RHS's Potentially harmful field "Harmful if eaten.  Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling" names no animal, and neither does Missouri Botanical Garden's "All parts of this plant are poisonous if ingested." (the auditor's browser reading).

is_edible false: RHS's Potentially harmful field reads "Harmful if eaten.  Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling", and NC State's human-scoped Poison block lists Roots and Seeds with stomach pain, nausea, vomiting and diarrhea; Missouri Botanical Garden's "All parts of this plant are poisonous if ingested." (the auditor's browser reading) agrees but is not cited. No admissible source describes any part as food, so no food use has to be weighed under the edibility rule.

is_houseplant false: NC State's Plant Type field lists Annual, Herbaceous Perennial and Poisonous, and the page's only indoor mention is storing the dug tuberous roots over winter, which is not houseplant culture. RHS's suggested planting locations are Patio and container plants and Flower borders and beds.

soil_drainage is moderate: NC State's structured Soil Drainage field is Occasionally Wet alone, but the prose says moist to occasionally wet, well-drained soil and that it grows in most soils, so this reads as a preference, not a consistently-wet requirement; the drought tolerant tag and Moderate drought tolerance counterweigh a wet reading.
water_regime and all watering fields left null: NC State gives no watering statement; the drought tolerance tag is a trait, not a watering instruction.

Only NC State's dedicated page was read during research. At audit and landing the other admissible dedicated pages were checked: RHS's (https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/11156/mirabilis-jalapa/details) and, by the auditor in a browser, Missouri Botanical Garden's (kempercode a595). They give no temperature, humidity, numeric pH, fertilizing or light-intensity values, so those fields stay null on the evidence. They do bear on the name, toxicity scope, edibility and size, which are disclosed in name_note, toxicity_detail, is_edible and the size note. NC State's Common Name(s) list for Gazania rigens is alphabetized (African Daisy, Gazania, Treasure Flower), and its page-title parenthetical shows the same order. Its first entry, African Daisy, also opens NC State's list for Gerbera jamesonii, and Gazania is the bare genus name, so this record lands the remaining entry, Treasure Flower. RHS's profile for Gazania rigens shows rigid treasure flower beneath the binomial and lists treasure flower under Other common names.
unknowns: Three admissible sources have a dedicated Gazania rigens page, and every field value in this record is taken from NC State's. MoBot Plant Finder (https://plantfinder.mobot.org/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?kempercode=a517) refuses this machine's non-browser fetches (connect and certificate errors) but renders in a browser; its readings below are the auditor's and are not cited. RHS's page is plant 86144 (https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/86144/gazania-rigens/details), Name Status Correct, synonym Gazania splendens. MoBot ('Sun: Full sun') and RHS's Position field ('Full sun') agree with full_sun. MoBot ('Height: 0.50 to 1.00 feet', 'Spread: 0.50 to 1.00 feet') matches NC State's 6-12 in. RHS's Max Height and Max Spread fields both read '0.1-0.5 metres' (about 4-20 in), and NC State's species Dimensions block is the anchor. Neither MoBot nor RHS addresses toxicity to cats or dogs or edibility. MoBot's watering text leans moister than NC State's; see the water_regime entry. MoBot's Common Name field reads 'treasure flower', the name landed here.
toxic_to_pets left null: NC State carries no poison block or Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tag on this page and no admissible page naming cats or dogs was read.
is_edible left null: no read admissible source addresses eating this plant.

soil_drainage left null: the admissible pages lean different ways. NC State's Soil Drainage field gives only 'Good Drainage', and its prose says 'Gazanias prefer sandy to average well-drained soils and are tolerant of loams and poor soils.' That is a range, not the sharp or sandy requirement 'fast' needs. NC State also warns 'Do not overwater to prevent root rot.' MoBot says 'Grow in sandy to average, well-drained soils in full sun.' and 'Overly moist soils can lead to root and stem rot.' (the auditor's browser reading). RHS's Moisture field reads 'Moist but well–drained or Well–drained', which this catalog would otherwise read as moderate.
soil_base left null: the page frames the plant both as a garden border/mass-planting plant and as best grown as an annual in containers or hanging baskets, with no soil-mix statement.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max left null: NC State's Soil pH field lists 'Acid (<6.0)' and 'Neutral (6.0-8.0)'. The acid band is open-ended, so it gives no floor. RHS's pH field for Gazania rigens reads 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral', so the closed top of NC State's neutral band is not used as a ceiling.

water_regime dry_surface_between is read from NC State's 'Allow the soil to dry between waterings' (no depth, 'surface' or 'thoroughly' stated), with 'Do not overwater to prevent root rot.' as the same-page caution. MoBot leans moister (the auditor's browser reading): its Water field reads 'Water: Medium', its Culture text says 'Tolerates some soil dryness, but prefers consistent moisture. Do not overwater, however.', and its Problems text warns 'Overly moist soils can lead to root and stem rot.' Letting only the surface dry is the reading both pages can bear, so dry_surface_between is kept and the disagreement is disclosed here. RHS's 'Water in prolonged dry spells' appears word for word in its Gazania linearis Cultivation text, so it is genus boilerplate and was not used. water_dry_down_target and the day-interval fields are left null because no source gives a dry-down depth or a number of days. NC State says gazanias 'are best grown as an annual in containers or hanging baskets' and 'can be planted the garden in borders or mass plantings'.

outdoor_sun_exposure is full_sun from NC State's structured Light field (its single value, 'Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)') and its description ('plant in full sun for best blooming'). MoBot's 'Sun: Full sun' (the auditor's browser reading) and RHS's Position field ('Full sun') agree. The hour figure inside NC State's Light value is the Toolbox's standard label for that category, identical on its Pentas lanceolata, Dianthus chinensis and Gerbera jamesonii pages. It is a minimum rather than a species maximum, so direct_sun_hours_max is null.

is_houseplant false: NC State says gazanias 'are best grown as an annual in containers or hanging baskets' and that 'Containers can be overwintered indoors or stem cuttings can be rooted and overwintered', which is overwintering, not houseplant culture; its Landscape Location field carries no Houseplants value.
Cultivar-specific statements on the NC State page (e.g. 'Talent Orange' attracts pollinators; 'Sundrop' tolerates dry conditions; cultivar heights) were not used for any field.
No temperature, humidity, light-fc, chill, or fertilizer figures were stated by the NC State page.
